name: Pale Payne's Grey
lede: Pale Payne's Grey is a soft, bluish grey built on the name of Payne's grey, the mixed watercolor wash painters use in place of black, and recorded by Ridgway in 1912.

sections.title: A paler wash
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* records this swatch as plate XLIX, hue 49 with four primes, tone f [1]. It takes its name from Payne's grey, the blue-black watercolor mix named for the eighteenth-century English painter William Payne, who favored it over flat black for softening shadows [1][2]. The American ISCC-NBS dictionary later filed the same swatch as block 185, a pale blue, and the German RAL system gives a near-duplicate of its own, Window Grey, only 2.2 units away [1].

In Munsell notation it reads as N 6.7, a near-neutral grey with almost no hue [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[pale-green-blue-grey]], [[light-blue-grey]], [[light-blue-grey]] and [[cadet-grey]], at 3.6, 3.9, 3.9 and 4.3 ΔE [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this grey in 504 of 23,781 paintings, 2.12 percent, more common than 76 percent of our named colors, as photographed [3]. It most often reads as a light tone rather than a shadow, in 56 percent of its appearances [3]. Claude Monet favors it most, in 9 of his 50 catalogued works here, nearly seven times the baseline rate for the museums those paintings come from [3]. The earliest dated example, from 1315, predates Ridgway's 1912 record of the name by nearly six centuries, so the match is a look-alike hue, not a trace of the pigment William Payne mixed, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].
